beats.text: A limit describes what nearby outputs approach, even when the target input itself is missing. This fraction is undefined at input one because its denominator is zero. We can still investigate values taken just to either side of that input.

Factor the numerator into x minus one times x plus one. At every allowed nearby input, the common nonzero factor cancels and the output equals x plus one. The simplified expression reveals a line with its original missing point retained.

As inputs approach one from either direction, these outputs approach two. That statement does not fill the hole or claim the original function equals two at one. A limit concerns nearby behavior; a function value concerns a particular allowed input.

Both directions must agree for a two-sided limit. Absolute x divided by x equals negative one to the left of zero and positive one to the right. Because those approaches disagree, there is no single two-sided limit at zero.

practice.prompt: For f(x)=x+4 except at x=2 where it is undefined, find the limit as x approaches two. Explain.
practice.answer: The nearby rule approaches six, so the limit is6 even though f(2) is undefined.

practice.prompt: Simplify (x²−100)/(x−10) near x=10 and determine its limit there.
practice.answer: Forx≠10 it equalsx+10; asx approaches10 the output approaches20.

practice.prompt: A function approaches three from the left of a point and negative two from the right. Can it have a two-sided limit there?
practice.answer: No. A two-sided limit requires the two one-sided limits to agree.

takeaway: Nearby agreement determines a limit; the point value and the two approaches must be distinguished.
scope: Removable gaps, valid simplification near a point, and one-sided agreement.
title: Introduction to limits
objective: Compare function values with the value approached from nearby inputs.
